primaryRequirement: A modern foreign language is compulsory from grade 1, but in grades 1 and 2 it is taught as an integrated compulsory exercise woven through other subjects — 32 annual lessons — rather than as a subject of its own. From grade 3, at around age 8, it becomes a standalone subject with one weekly lesson in each of grades 3 and 4. The curriculum specifies a 'modern foreign language' without naming which, leaving the choice to schools. The governing document is the Primary School Curriculum, Federal Law Gazette 134/1963 as amended by Federal Law Gazette II 269/2023 of 15 September 2023, in force from 2023/24. (Eurydice, Eurypedia — Austria)
secondaryRequirement: Two foreign languages become compulsory for all students in general education only at upper secondary level, from age 14 or 15. upperSecondary: Once compulsory foreign language learning has begun it continues until the last or the penultimate year of upper secondary education, as it does in every European system except Malta. (Eurydice, Key data on teaching languages at school in Europe – 2023 edition)
languagesOffered: Steering documents also name Czech, Slovak and Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian, the last taught as a single language. The number of languages schools may provide is among the highest in Europe at all three levels. Content and language integrated learning (CLIL) is delivered in these combinations: German + Arabic, Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian or English (ISCED 1–3); German + Spanish (ISCED 1–2); German + French (ISCED 1); German + Chinese or Polish (ISCED 2); German + Burgenland Croatian, Hungarian or Slovenian (ISCED 1–3); German + Czech or Slovak (ISCED 1–2). assessment: At the end of lower secondary education the second foreign language is expected to reach A2 for spoken production and A1 for spoken interaction; the same level is expected of the first and second foreign languages at that point. docLinks.label: Language Trends England 2024 (Collen & Duff, British Council)

primaryRequirement: The National Curriculum, which all local-authority-maintained schools must teach, requires an ancient or modern foreign language at Key Stage 2 (years 3–6, ages 7–11). There is no requirement at Key Stage 1 (ages 5–7). Academies are not obliged to follow the National Curriculum, though in practice many do. In 2023/24, 99 per cent of responding state primary schools had taught a language within curriculum time, the same figure as the year before, and over 80 per cent had been doing so for more than five years. One responding school in four reported that time allocated to languages had been reduced by pupils spending extra time on literacy and numeracy. Language Trends England 2024 (Collen and Duff, British Council; 1 324 schools surveyed January–March 2024 — 603 state primary, 601 state secondary, 120 independent).
secondaryRequirement: A modern foreign language is required at Key Stage 3 (years 7–9, ages 11–14). There is no requirement at Key Stage 4 (ages 14–16), although the English Baccalaureate accountability measure, introduced in 2010, encourages a language GCSE alongside English, mathematics, the sciences and a humanity. Language Trends England 2024 (Collen and Duff, British Council; 1 324 schools surveyed January–March 2024 — 603 state primary, 601 state secondary, 120 independent).
upperSecondary: No language is required after age 14. Post-16, 47 per cent of responding state secondary schools had language provision of their own and a further 8 per cent had sharing arrangements with another school, against 89 per cent of independent schools. For the fifth year running Spanish was the most popular A-level language, in contrast to primary and GCSE level where French remains the most taught. Language Trends England 2024 (Collen and Duff, British Council; 1 324 schools surveyed January–March 2024 — 603 state primary, 601 state secondary, 120 independent).
languagesOffered: In responding state primary schools in 2023/24, French was taught in 64 per cent of schools at Key Stage 2 — down nearly 10 percentage points on 2023 — followed by Spanish at 31 per cent, German at 2–3 per cent and Latin at 3 per cent. Latin appeared in the 'top four' for a second year; of the schools teaching it, just over half said all Key Stage 2 pupils had access. Italian, Arabic and Mandarin each appeared in about 1 per cent of schools, and British Sign Language and Hebrew in 1–2 per cent. Language Trends England 2024 (Collen and Duff, British Council; 1 324 schools surveyed January–March 2024 — 603 state primary, 601 state secondary, 120 independent).
curriculumTime: The National Curriculum sets no minimum hours for languages. Among responding independent schools, about a third allocate one to two hours and a third two to three hours of class time per week at Key Stage 3; by Key Stage 4 around two thirds allocate two to three hours and nearly 30 per cent more than three. Comparable figures were not collected for state schools. Language Trends England 2024 (Collen and Duff, British Council; 1 324 schools surveyed January–March 2024 — 603 state primary, 601 state secondary, 120 independent).
assessment: GCSE at 16 and A-level at 18. Reformed GCSEs in French, German and Spanish were taught from September 2024 for first award in summer 2026, following the MFL Pedagogy Review; their linguistic content is restricted to the most frequent vocabulary of each language — 1 700 words at Higher Tier and 1 200 at Foundation — with any other words on the paper glossed. The reform applies only to those three languages and only to awarding organisations in England, so a GCSE in French, German or Spanish taken with a Northern Irish or Welsh awarding organisation is a different qualification. On EBacc entry, 39 per cent of pupils were entered for the full English Baccalaureate in 2022/23; of the 86 per cent who entered four or more components, nearly 90 per cent did not take a language GCSE. Language Trends England 2024 (Collen and Duff, British Council; 1 324 schools surveyed January–March 2024 — 603 state primary, 601 state secondary, 120 independent).

Among state secondary schools 33 per cent called it a major issue and 31 per cent a minor one, with 30 per cent reporting no issue; in independent schools 48 per cent reported no issue. Language Trends England 2024 (Collen and Duff, British Council; 1 324 schools surveyed January–March 2024 — 603 state primary, 601 state secondary, 120 independent).

Four per cent of state secondary and 8 per cent of independent schools facilitate the teaching of community languages during the school day.
